title.en: The Two Lizards and the First Flute

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Two Lizards'

summary.en: Nagari the lizard could whistle one sweet note and drew the women round him; plain-spoken Webubu, lonely, cut a slim piece of hollow bamboo and pierced holes in it — thus was the first duraio, the flute, born. His music drew the women one by one away from Nagari, until the platform of Webubu crashed under them all and the tioba trees have leaned earthward ever since.
summary.zh: 蜥蜴納加里會吹出甜美的『嗚——』聲，引得村中女子圍坐聽曲；言語笨拙的韋布布孤身無伴，忽得一計：他截一段空心竹、鑽上小孔——第一支杜拉伊奧（笛）由此而生。笛聲一起，女子們一個個借口離去，投奔笛聲，納加里獨坐原處。眾女湧上韋布布建在迪奧巴樹頂的樂台，不堪重負，轟然墜地——至今迪奧巴樹皆朝地面傾斜。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910), tales told to the author in Wedau and translated; Wamira heritage.

passages.text: In the old days there lived two lizards, Webubu and Nagari. Webubu was plain of speech, and moreover was unable to cry aloud, but Nagari, by stretching his long neck, could produce a sweet low sound, somewhat after the manner of a whistle. Nagari longed for companions, so he stretched his neck, and cried, 'U-u-u-u-u.' Then many women, hearing the sweet sound, flocked to where Nagari sat, and listened to his music. This pleased Nagari, and he continued to sound his long note, and the women sat so still, one might have thought them dead or sleeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Two Lizards' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Webubu, on the contrary, had no one to cheer him in his loneliness. 'What can I do,' he said, 'to draw women to me as Nagari has done? I have not a sweet voice as he has.' As he was speaking a thought grew up in his heart, and he began to act. He cut a slim piece of hollow bamboo, and pierced small holes in it. Thus was the first duraio or flute born. Webubu then built himself a platform high in a corkwood tree, which we call tioba, on the beach, and seating himself there, he began to play his duraio. High and sweet were the notes he sent forth; the listening women cried, 'Deafen us not with thine U, when we would fain hear this strange music!' Then one woman made bold to rise, and saying, 'I shall return,' went to seek the sweet music — and she lied, for she never returned. And so with each woman, until Nagari was left sitting alone as he had been at the beginning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Two Lizards' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now Webubu was still playing his duraio on the platform he had built in the tioba tree, when the women came in sight. He was alarmed for the safety of his frail platform, when he saw these many people advancing, and he cried, 'Come not up into the tree. Remain below, I beseech you, O women!' But the women were consumed with eagerness to be close to the music which had taken their hearts, and they climbed, all of them, until they were upon the platform of Webubu. Then straightway what he had feared came to pass, and Webubu, and his duraio, and the multitude of women fell crashing through the branches of the tioba to the ground beneath. And from that hour until now, all tioba trees lean towards the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Two Lizards' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: How the Turtle Got His Shell (Ker's Telling)

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'How the Turtle Got His Shell'

summary.en: The Turtle and the Wallaby feasted in Binama the hornbill's garden; the wallaby leapt away, the turtle was caught for the feast, and won the children's help with soft words — crawling in their father's shell necklace, armlets, and a great wooden bowl. Diving from the stones of the pursuing birds, he lost armlets and necklace but the bowl never broke: all turtles carry Binama's bowl on their backs to this day.
summary.zh: 龜與袋鼠偷入犀鳥比納馬的園中飽食蕉蔗；袋鼠一躍而逃，龜被縛於架上待宰。他向看守的孩子們柔聲求情，借來父親最貴的貝殼項鍊、兩枚貝釧與一隻大木碗，披掛表演，逗得孩子們大笑。聽見大人回村，他直奔入海；群鳥沿岸擲石，先碎左釧，再碎右釧，又砸斷項鍊之繩；最後的大石紛紛落在木碗上，碗卻分毫無損。龜遠遁——至今龜背所負，仍是比納馬家中的木碗。

passages.text: Long ago, our fathers have told us, the Turtle and the Wallaby were friends. Now on a certain day, the Turtle was hungry, and asked his friend to go with him to the beach and from thence to the hornbill's garden, where was much sugarcane and where bananas also were plentiful. This they did, and fed plentifully on all that was there. The Wallaby trod upon the stalks of the bananas and bowed them to the ground that his friend might eat. Thus did he also to the tall sugarcane and the orabu, the flowering rush. And they both did eat and their hunger was stayed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Turtle Got His Shell' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now while they were eating the birds were at work in their gardens, tilling the ground. When the work was finished they dug up much taro and returned to the village to cook their food. Then said Binama the hornbill, 'Let one of you go down to the beach and bring sea water that our food may be salted.' But his word bare no fruit, for one by one the birds made excuse, fearing lest an enemy lay in wait. At last the wagtail arose and ran to make ready. And as he went he leapt from side to side the better to avoid the foe, if foe there were. In a little he came to Binama's garden and saw the Turtle and Wallaby feeding. Their hearts trembled; nevertheless the Turtle made bold and said to the wagtail, 'Thy master has bidden us eat of his bananas that our hunger may be stayed.' Now the wagtail knew in his heart that they lied, but he answered never a word, but filled his bottles with sea water and ran back to the village by another way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Turtle Got His Shell' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Wallaby lifted up his head and seeing nought but enemies round about him, tarried not but leaped mightily and escaped. The Turtle could not jump, so he crawled with haste into a yam patch and hid himself under the leaves. But the birds hunted for him diligently and at last found him and dragged him forth, and tied him to a pole and thus carried him to Binama's house, where they laid him upon a shelf till the morrow. The next day Binama called his servants together and all went to dig food to make a feast when they should slay the Turtle. None were in the house but the children whom Binama had set to guard the captive. Then the Turtle made his voice soft, and called the children unto him. 'Loosen my bonds, O children,' quoth he, 'that we may play together.' Now the children knew not what was in the Turtle's mind, and they did as he bade them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Turtle Got His Shell' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: He crawled down from the shelf, and stretched himself, for he was stiff and sore. Then he said to the children, 'Where are your ornaments? Leave the poor ones in the basket, and bring forth only the good ones, that I may see them.' The children ran to the place where Binama kept his ornaments, and brought forth a long necklace of shell money, also two shell armlets and a wooden bowl, and laid them before the Turtle. He forthwith wound the necklace many times round his neck, and put on both the shell armlets; moreover the bowl he fastened upon his back. The children laughed to watch his ungainly form decorated with their father's ornaments. But on a sudden he heard voices and knew the men were drawing near; then he ran swiftly to the sea, and hasted to dive. The birds called, 'Show thyself now. Lift up thine head.' This did the Turtle, and the angry birds cast great stones into the sea, and the left armlet which the Turtle wore was shattered. So he dived, but they called again, and a stone fell upon the right armlet and brake it into small pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'How the Turtle Got His Shell' (1910); not verbatim.

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Man Who Left Heaven'

summary.en: Jealous companions cast out the man whose string of shell money outmeasured theirs; winds drove his lime-gourd boat to the foot of the mountains behind which the stars rise. Magamaia and Deboroia would not stay for him, but the morning star Maratomtom bore him up to heaven, where a damsel took him to husband. Seeing his own village's palms below, he let himself down to earth by a shell-money cord — and burned his faithless companions in the potuma, the club-house; their charred bodies clinging to the roof became the flying-foxes whose cry is the cry of a soul in pain.
summary.zh: 貝殼錢串最長的男人遭同伴嫉妒而棄於荒灘；他乘漂流的檳榔灰罐隨風至眾星之山。星星 Magamaia 與 Deboroia 都說『再等等』，只有晨星馬拉托姆托姆垂憐，攜他升天。天上佳人招他為夫，生子育女。一日父子以矛擲戲，矛落在地上他自家村中的椰樹頂上——他望鄉心切，以貝錢搓繩縋落人間（自此天上貝錢最美，人間的黯淡粗劣）。妻當他已死多年，見他歸來大喜。他設宴款待昔日負心之人，將他們關進男子會所，四面縱火；烈焰中他們攀附梁頂而亡，屍身化作狐蝠——至今棲於高處，其叫聲便是痛苦靈魂之聲。

passages.text: In a certain village lived some men who longed for strings of shell money. So they took counsel together and agreed to go to a far village and there barter store of betel nuts for what their souls desired. They set forth therefore, and in time reached the land where shell money was to be found. One of their number tarried with the canoe, while the others climbed the hill. In a little while a child came down to the beach near where the canoe lay, and to him spake the man; and he followed the child to his father's house, where he received much shell money. Then he coiled the strings of money in a water bottle, and went down to the canoe, where he awaited his companions. They were not long in coming, and glad were their voices as they spake of the long strings of money they had received. And all set out for their home. But on the way they were disputing whose string was the longest, and desired to land that they might know whose was the best.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Left Heaven' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was a desolate shore on which they landed. A pandanus grew near, and one by one the men hung their strings of money over its branches and watched as they hung near the ground. And now it was the turn of the man who had stayed behind to measure his. But he hung his not on the branch of the pandanus, but on the top; and it lay upon the ground, and many coils were yet in the water bottle. When the men saw this and that their friend's money so far surpassed theirs, some of them were jealous, and some were sad, some others were angry, and many coveted it greatly. But on this were all of one mind. No longer should he travel with them. So they launched the canoe, and told the man with the long necklace that he might not go with them. The man sought for a way of escape, but found none. Then he bethought him of the lime gourd he carried over his shoulder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Left Heaven' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Night fell, and Magamaia rose above the sea. 'Stay but a moment,' cried the man, 'and let me hold thee and together we will mount.' But Magamaia answered, 'Tarry a little; our friend Deboroia will soon be here.' Then it was the turn of Deboroia. 'Stay but a moment,' cried the man again. But Deboroia answered even as had Magamaia, 'Tarry a little, for Maratomtom (the morning star) will soon be here.' The man's heart was hot within him for grief that no star would have pity on him in his sad plight, and he wept sore. But as he wept and lamented, Maratomtom rose and hearkened to his cry. The man held fast and Maratomtom and he rose together high into the heaven. The man let go his hold and lighted where much people were gathered together. The people of heaven marvelled greatly when the man showed himself unto them, and one damsel looking on him required that he should be her husband. So were they married, and for a time the man forgot the land which he had left. In due time a son was born to them, and grew and waxed strong.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Left Heaven' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now it fell upon a day that the lad cut many spears and brought them unto his father that he might sharpen them for him. This he did and the lad, seeing many coconuts far below him upon the earth, speared them from his home in the heaven. But the father was loth to make new darts, and said, 'Where are the ones I made thee?' Then he too looked down and saw upon the earth the tops of the palms of his own village. And his heart died at the sight, for he longed with an exceeding great longing to visit his land once more. So he took a long cord of pandanus and strung upon it the shell money which was not of the best; but the red and large and round he placed in a heap upon the ground, and commanded that it should be laid up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Left Heaven' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Feast in the Potuma and the Flying-Foxes

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Man Who Left Heaven'

summary.en: Come down to earth after years in heaven, the man saluted his false companions with fair words, bade them to a feast, closed the doorways of the potuma and fired it at each corner. Their cries were stilled, and their charred bodies clinging to the roof became the flying-foxes which ever haunt high places, whose cry is the cry of a soul in pain. And a taboo on his coco palms had mourned him as dead all those years.
summary.zh: 男人自天上歸來，先向昔日棄他之人致以美言問候，並邀他們赴宴。宴備妥後，他自己不進會所，卻把 potuma（男子會所）的各門緊閉，再於四角縱火。火高煙濃，賓客遍尋出路不得；慘呼漸息，燒焦的屍體攀附在屋頂上——化作狐蝠。狐蝠至今棲居高處，其叫聲便是痛苦的靈魂之聲。而這些年裡，人間的妻子早把他當作亡夫服喪，連他名下的椰樹都被下了禁忌。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage. Second half of the Man Who Left Heaven cycle.

passages.text: Now, as the man was thus seated on high, it came to pass that the daughter who had been born to him upon earth came to gaze on her father's coconuts. She knew she might but look, and that to taste was forbidden, for her mother mourned her father as one long dead, and a taboo had been laid on all the coco palms which had been his. But, as she gazed, she discerned a man seated among the leaves, and, looking steadfastly on him, she knew him to be her father, and straightway ran to her mother and told her the tidings. But her mother answered, 'How can this be, my daughter? Thy father is dead, and I have mourned for him these many years. It is another man thou hast seen.' Nevertheless, at her daughter's word she went out and found even as she had said. Then was her heart glad, and she bade her husband come down and enter the house that she might make ready food for him to eat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Left Heaven' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Being now refreshed, he minded him of the companions who had aforetime treated him evilly, and appeared unto them with many fair words and kindly greetings. He also bade them to a feast he was about to make. Much taro was boiled, and a pig was slain, and, all being made ready, the guests were gathered together in the potuma, which is the club-house. But the man himself did not enter, for he desired to take vengeance on his enemies. So he closed the doorways of the potuma and made them fast that no one might chance to escape, and then he set fire to each corner of the house. The flames rose high and thick smoke filled the potuma, as the feasters looked for a way of escape. But they looked in vain, and soon their cries were stilled, and their charred bodies clinging to the roof of the potuma were changed into flying foxes, which ever haunt high places, and whose cry is the cry of a soul in pain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Man Who Left Heaven' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Dabedabe the Good and the Bones of His Mother

region.en: Bou, hill country above Wamira, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉山地之布村（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Dabedabe the Good'

summary.en: The sow that farrowed five pigs and one man-child was cooked for the workmen at her son Dabedabe's garden; he gathered her bones in a mat and carried them away to Qamana, and at the river's bank flung them on the stones — they became men and pigs in hundreds. With them he ransomed the captives bound for a Walaga cannibal feast, and from that day men are spared and pigs slain when a feast is made.
summary.zh: 布村一戶的母豬在林中產下五豬一男嬰；男孩達貝達貝被主人抱回撫養。他長成後請村人助墾新園，好養育豬母；主人卻殺了豬母款待助工。達貝達貝命人把骨頭盡數留在席布上，收拾進袋，離村遠行，直至不見母親村莊的卡馬納。他孤身住於洞穴，得一小童照料瘡傷。聞村人將開 Walaga 宴——以人為食——他怒而赴河邊，把袋中母骨奮力擲上石頭：骨化為人，立聽號令；再擲，化為成群之豬。他命新造之人砍桿縛豬，趕赴宴所，對宴主說：『放了你綁著的人，我把這些豬都給你。』宴主貪豬而從之。自那日起，巴布亞人開宴皆殺豬而不殺人——如無達貝達貝，講這故事的說書人也早被縛上木桿吃掉了。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); Wamira heritage. The tale aitions the substitution of pigs for human victims at feasts.

passages.text: This is a tale of the men of Bou, which is in the hill country to the south of Wamira. A certain man had a pig, which left him and gave birth to her young in the bush. Now five of them were pigs like their mother, but the sixth was a man child, and him his mother loved best of all. Day by day did the six follow her as she sought their food in the bush, and after a time, their footprints being many, the men of Bou knew where they were hiding. So they took pig nets and set out to catch them. Now the owner of the old pig looked at the footprints, and seeing the footprints of a child among them said, 'Ye may keep the young pigs when they are caught, save only the one whose marks are these.' So the nets were made ready, and the five little pigs were soon caught. But the old mother, fearing danger, had hidden the man child, and he was not therefore caught in the net.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now it came to pass when the boy was now grown that on a day he heard his mother crying for food, and he resolved to make a garden that he might grow food to give her when she was hungry. So he called to the men of the village, and asked them to help him make his garden; and the lad, whose name was Dabedabe, set out with many men for the plantation. Soon had they cleared the ground, and then they made a fence about it. Now while they were fencing the garden, the owner of the pigs went back to the village, and made ready food, that the men who had helped Dabedabe might eat in the evening when they returned. And as he desired that they should eat and be full he killed the old pig whose son was Dabedabe, and cooked her flesh with the taro. And when the men returned from the garden he said, 'Sit ye down and eat, for supper is ready.' Now Dabedabe watched while the man did this, and he said, 'What is the flesh in the pot?' 'It is pig's flesh, my son,' said the man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Dabedabe went into the house and brought forth a mat, and spread it in the sight of all, saying, 'When ye eat throw no bone away, but lay all upon the mat which I have spread before you.' And they did even as he had said. Then when all had eaten Dabedabe wrapped up the bones of the pig, and slung the bundle on his shoulder, and said, 'Friends, we were to-day making a garden that I might have wherewithal to give my mother to eat when she hungered, but she hath been slain, and ye have eaten her, therefore I can no longer stay here, but must leave you. Farewell.' Thus he left the village, and journeyed until he came to Peubua; there he sat down, and would fain have remained there, but, turning himself, he saw his mother's village behind him, and his heart burned. Therefore he rose up, and journeyed until he came to Reborebo; and in like manner, on looking behind him, he could see his mother's village in the distance, and for grief at the sight he tarried not, but went on until he came to Doula.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the men of Qamana would not suffer him to abide in their village, because his body was covered with noisome sores. Therefore, as the rain was heavy, he sought shelter in a cave, where he dwelt alone. And after not many days he called a child to him, who abode with him in the cave and dressed his sores, and cooked his food; so it was that his sores were healed and strength came back to him. Now it came to pass that, as he and the boy sat together in the cave, they heard the voice of a drum in the village. 'What meaneth the voice of the drum which I hear?' 'The men of Qamana are dancing because of the feast they are about to make.' 'On what are they going to feast?' 'On men,' quoth the boy, 'and the name of the feast is Walaga.' Dabedabe's heart grew hot within him at this word, and he went into the village and sought for the giver of the feast, and found him standing by a long row of poles on which burdens were strapped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ransom of the Walaga Feast

region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞卡馬納（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'Dabedabe the Good'

summary.en: 'Do not this thing, I pray thee,' besought Dabedabe, 'but tarry a little while I go to the river.' There he flung his mother's bones violently upon a stone, and they became men and stood before him; again he flung the rest, and they became pigs, a great number. Bound to the poles they had cut, the pig-men came in a long line to the feast: 'Set free the men whom ye have bound, and I will give thee these pigs which thou seest.' From that day men are spared and pigs slain at feasts, and Qamana and Bou have abundance of pigs to this day.
summary.zh: 『求你莫行此事，』達貝達貝懇求道，『且稍等，我去去河邊便回。』他到河邊打開口袋，取母骨猛擲石上——骨化為人，立於面前聽令；他命他們入林砍桿，一砍再砍，直至夠數；又把餘骨擲上河岸之石，化作大群之豬。人們把豬縛上長桿，肩扛成行赴宴。達貝達貝對宴主說：『放了你綁著的那些人，我這些豬都給你。』宴主見豬心動，依言解縛。眾人歡宴，塗髮插羽，分食豬肉。自那日起直到如今，巴布亞人開宴殺豬而不殺人；卡馬納與布村至今豬群興旺。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Ker 1910); second half of the Dabedabe cycle.

passages.text: 'Do not this thing, I pray thee,' besought Dabedabe, 'but tarry a little while I go to the river. I shall return.' Then he hasted and returned to the cave, and took his bag in his hand, and went down to the river. There he opened the bag, and took from it some of his mother's bones which he had placed within it on the day that he took leave of his people at Bou. And he flung the bones violently upon a stone, and they became men, and stood before him to hear what he would say. Then said he to them, 'Go ye into the bush and cut many poles, and fetch them hither.' So they went and cut many poles, as he had said, but lo, when they brought them to Dabedabe he said, 'These are too few. Go ye and cut more.' Then they came again carrying more poles, but not yet were they enough, and he sent them forth a third time to fetch more, and now were there as many as he wanted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: He therefore took the rest of his mother's bones out of his bag and threw them violently upon the stones by the river's bank, and they became pigs, a great number. Then he bade the men who stood near bind the pigs to the poles they had cut, and he himself returned swiftly to the giver of the feast and cried, 'Cook now my gwada of plantains, and anoint it with coconut, for I and my men will soon be here.' When he had said this he returned to the river and bade the men carry the pigs, which had been bound to the poles, upon their shoulders to the feast. Thus did they, and many marvelled as they saw the long line of men, each bearing the end of a pole upon his shoulder, a pig being bound to each pole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now when they reached the place set apart for the feast, Dabedabe said to his men, 'Set your burdens upon the ground,' and they did so. Then said he to the giver of the feast, 'Set free the men whom ye have bound, and I will give thee these pigs which thou seest.' And the giver of the feast, greatly desiring the pigs, did as Dabedabe had said, and unloosed the bonds of the men which lay upon the ground waiting to be slain. Then did all make merry, and tire their hair, and hang many ornaments of shell and feathers upon themselves, and did eat of the pigs which Dabedabe had given them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: And in truth if Dabedabe had not done this thing, we of Papua, yea, even I who tell the tale, would have been bound upon poles and eaten at the feasts of our enemies. But from that day even until now are men spared and pigs slain when a feast is made, and at Qamana as also at Bou are abundance of pigs to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'Dabedabe the Good' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dancing Dame and the Drum of the Waves

region.en: Wamira coast, British New Guinea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 英屬新幾內亞瓦米拉海岸（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 1910

source.work: Annie Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales (London: Macmillan, 1910), 'The Dancing Dame'

summary.en: A blind grandmother sent daily for salt water heard the waves beat on the coral cliffs and took it for the drum of a feast; she laid down her staff and danced on the beach. Her daughter-in-law set the child to spy, and mocked her — 'How loud is thy drum, O dame, seeing it is beaten by a thousand waves!' — and at the taunt and the cruel laughter the old woman grew cold with shame, fell to the earth, and her spirit left her. The loud beat of the waves is the voice of the blind woman's drum still.
summary.zh: 盲眼老嫗每日奉命下灘取鹹水，忽聞濤聲拍打珊瑚崖，誤以為是宴樂之鼓，便放下手杖在灘上獨舞至倦。媳婦疑其怠惰，遣幼子窺探；得知真相後母子大笑，嘲道：『你的鼓聲好響啊，老婆子——一千道浪替你打鼓！』老嫗聽了這嘲弄與殘忍的笑聲，羞愧徹骨，寒徹周身，倒地而亡。至今浪聲大作時，人們便說：『聽！那是盲嫗的鼓。』

passages.text: In a certain village lived a woman and her little son, and with them dwelt an old woman, who was the child's grandmother, and she was blind. Now her daughter-in-law, not being willing that the dame should eat unless she also worked, bade her fetch salt water each day from the beach that the food might be salted. This did the old woman, and she went never astray, for there was but one path to the beach, and with her staff in her hand she went bravely. Now when her eyes were open in the old days, the dame lived ever upon the mountains, and thus had never seen the sea. And it came to pass that on a certain day when she went down to the beach, she heard the waves beating upon the coral cliffs and fancied it was the voice of the drum which she heard. So laying down her staff she fell to dancing, and ceased not until she was weary. Then filling the coconut water bottle with salt water she went back to the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Dancing Dame' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the morrow did she the same as on the day before. Again the waves beat upon the coral, and again the dame thought it to be the voice of the drum. And this time she danced for so long that her daughter-in-law was very angry, and ceased not to scold her for not returning to the house until the night was nigh. And as the dame would not tell her for what cause she remained so long, she resolved to set a watch on her the next day. Therefore when the dame set out on the morrow her daughter-in-law said to her little son, 'Follow thy grandmother to the beach, and bring me word again why she tarrieth so long.' And the child did as his mother bade him, and sat down at a distance on the beach to see what the dame would do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Dancing Dame' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he saw her lay down her staff and dance to the sound of the waves which beat upon the coral. And when he had watched her for long, and saw that she ceased not to dance, he ran back to his mother and said, 'My grandmother is even now dancing alone upon the beach. There is no voice of drum, nor any people, but only the waves beating upon the coral.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Dancing Dame' (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the woman laughed for scorn that the dame should spend her time in such a manner, and when she returned bearing the sea water she cried, 'How loud is thy drum, O dame, seeing it is beaten by a thousand waves!' And she and her child laughed loudly at the blind woman. She heard the taunt and the cruel laughter, and grew cold with shame, and fell to the earth, and her spirit left her. And now when the waves beat loud upon the coral we say, 'Hark! it is the voice of the blind woman's drum.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ker, Papuan Fairy Tales, 'The Dancing Dame' (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Tabuikor's Flood: The Woman Who Made All Lands
title.zh: 塔布伊科爾洪水：造萬地之婦

region.zh: 新不列顛卡巴比亞聖泉（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, 1910, ch. XIV

source.work: George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians: Their Life-Histories Described and Compared (London: Macmillan, 1910), ch. XIV 'History, Mythology'

summary.en: Tabuikor the woman made the land at Kababiai while her two sons worked it — until they caught her mingling her own water into their food. They ate her tainted tuba before her face, and in her anger she rolled away the stone that kept the sea confined: water poured out in a great flood, the origin of the sea. Then they sprinkled pieces of earth upon the waters and other islands came up; sprinkled them on the land and trees, and animals and men grew. Her sacred spring remains at Kababiai, where none dare bathe or drink, for an immense fish lives in it that will come when they call.
summary.zh: 婦人塔布伊科爾在卡巴比亞造地，兩個兒子耕作；她煮芋時竟以己溺調羹。二子察覺，商定計策，當面奪食她那摻了穢物的芋。她大怒，把一直鎮住海洋的那塊石頭推開——海水傾瀉而出，氾濫成災，海由此而生。二子又取地之碎塊撒於水上，別的島嶼隨之浮起；再撒於陸地，樹木、走獸與人類由此而生。卡巴比亞的聖泉至今猶在，村人不敢在其中沐浴或飲用——泉中住著一條大魚，喚之即來。

sensitivity.note: Missionary record (Brown 1910); New Britain heritage. Flood-cluster cross-ref.

passages.text: Tabui Kor was a woman, Tilik and Tarai were two men, her sons, whether born or not is not clear. They lived at Kababiai, where the sacred spring is, and from this they made the land (not yet the world). The woman made it and the two men worked it. The men worked whilst the woman cooked the tuba or cabbage. The two men, however, found out that their food tasted very nasty, and so one day they agreed that one of them should work with both axes so as to make the woman believe that they were both working, whilst the other went and hid so as to watch the cooking. He went and saw the woman make water into their cabbage, and put pure sea water into her own tuba. He said to himself, 'Alas indeed for us two if she continues doing that to our food.' He went and told his brother, and they agreed upon a certain action which they would take.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they came to dinner they took the woman's tuba while she was not looking and substituted theirs instead, which she had mixed with her urine because she was too lazy to go for sea water. They snatched away her food and ate it. She protested, but they ate it still. Then she got angry and went and rolled away the stone which had hitherto kept the sea confined, and the water and sea poured out in a great flood, and this was the origin of the sea. They afterwards took pieces of the earth and sprinkled them on the sea and other islands came up. Then they sprinkled this also on the land and trees, and animals and men grew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kababiai have the spring yet, but they never bathe in it or drink of it, and were very frightened when our boys drank of it. They say that an immense fish lives in it which will come when they call it, but it failed to do so when our boys got them to call, though they called long and loudly enough. It will be seen from this that the belief in New Britain that the creator of all things was a woman was the same as that which is held in many other Melanesian groups. This Tabuikor seems to have had also the name of Ne Kidong; she was the woman who made all lands, and to whom the natives prayed when an eclipse of the sun or moon took place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: To Kabanana the Good Workman and To Purgo the Bad
title.zh: 巧匠卡巴納那與拙工普爾戈

region.en: Duke of York Islands, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛約克公爵群島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, 1910, ch. XIV

source.work: George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians: Their Life-Histories Described and Compared (London: Macmillan, 1910), ch. XIV 'History, Mythology'

summary.en: In the New Britain mythology, To Kabanana was the first man and the maker of all things good and useful; To Purgo (on Duke of York) or To Purungo/To Purukelel (on New Britain) spoilt all the works of To Kabanana and was the author of all evil. Their names are used to this day: To Kabanana means a good workman, To Purgo a bad one — the local counterparts of Tagaro and Suqe of the northern New Hebrides.
summary.zh: 新不列顛神話中，卡巴納那為首人，造一切善物與有用之物；普爾戈（約克公爵島稱法；新不列顛島稱普魯恩戈或普魯克勒勒爾）專壞卡巴納那之功，乃一切禍惡之源。二人之名至今日常使用：稱能工為卡巴納那，稱拙工為普爾戈——恰與新赫布里底北部的塔加羅與蘇蓋相對應。

sensitivity.note: Missionary record (Brown 1910); cross-ref to-kabinana/to-karvuvu (Dixon recension of the same cycle).

passages.text: There were two other characters in their mythology, the one called To Kabanana, who was supposed to have been the first man, and the maker of all things good and useful; and another called on Duke of York To Pulgo, and on New Britain To Purungo or To Purukelel, who spoilt all the works of To Kabanana and was the author of all evil. The names of these two men are continually used to-day, the former meaning a good workman and the latter a bad one. It is interesting to note that these two personages have their counterparts in other Melanesian groups. In the northern New Hebrides, Tagaro and Suqe occupy the same relative positions. Tagaro wanted everything to be good, and would have no pain or evil; Suqe would have all things bad. At Whitsuntide Island whatever Tagaro did or made was right, Suqe was always wrong.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: To Kadol, Limlimanawin, and the Head in the Water Hole
title.zh: 卡多爾、林利馬溫與水潭中的頭顱

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, 1910, ch. XIV

source.work: George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians: Their Life-Histories Described and Compared (London: Macmillan, 1910), ch. XIV 'History, Mythology'

summary.en: To Kadol found a little boy and girl who had run away from their angry mother and took them home; his wife Limlimanawin, jealous of the girl, feigned sickness, murdered the boy while the parents were away, ate part of the body and hid the head. Detected, she was burnt with her house — but the boy's head, thrown into a water hole, was visited again and again by the woman's spirit, who at last restored him to life, decked him with ornaments, took him back to To Kadol, and tried to prove her innocence.
summary.zh: 卡多爾拾得因偷芒果被母責罵而出逃的一對小兄妹，帶回家中；其妻林利馬溫嫉妒那女孩，佯裝生病留在家中，趁機殺害男孩、食其部分遺體、藏起頭顱。事發後，她連人帶屋被燒。男孩的頭被拋入水潭；那女人的魂靈卻一再回到潭邊探視，終於使他復活，為他披掛飾物，帶他回到卡多爾面前，並竭力為自己辯白無辜。

passages.text: To Kadol was a mythical person who found a little boy and girl who had run away from their mother in the plantation, because she was angry with them for having taken her mango. He took them home and his wife Limlimanawin wanted to eat the boy, and was very jealous of the girl who was watched by To Kadol. She pretended to be sick, stayed at home with the children, murdered the boy, ate part of the body, and hid the head. When detected she was burnt, together with the house in which she was. The boy's head was thrown into a water hole and was frequently visited by the spirit of the woman who eventually restored him to life, decked him out with ornaments, took him to To Kadol and tried to establish her innocence in the matter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Ya Dapal on the Rising Tide
title.zh: 潮漲之巖上的雅達帕爾

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, 1910, ch. XIV

source.work: George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians: Their Life-Histories Described and Compared (London: Macmillan, 1910), ch. XIV 'History, Mythology'

summary.en: A mythical woman named Ia (or Ya) Dapal ran away from her jealous and angry husband to a rock in the sea. As the tide rose her husband entreated her to come on shore, but she refused unless he would come and escort her — even when she could only speak by springing up out of the water. Thus she died; and her name is now used, by those who know the tradition, for an obstinate woman, especially a runaway wife.
summary.zh: 神話女子雅達帕爾因丈夫嫉妒動怒而出逃，避居海上孤岩。潮水漲起，丈夫在岸上懇求她回來；她卻說除非他親自下海來接——哪怕那時她只能躍出水面方能開口。丈夫終究未去，她便溺亡於漲潮之中。知此傳說的人至今用『雅達帕爾』來稱呼固執的女子，尤其是私奔之妻。

passages.text: A mythical woman was named Ia (or Ya) Dapal who ran away from her jealous and angry husband to a rock in the sea. As the tide rose her husband entreated her to go on shore, but she refused to do so unless he would come and escort her even when she could only speak by springing up out of the water. Thus she died and her name is now used, by those who know the tradition, for an obstinate woman, especially if she be a runaway wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Kaia and Nara: Spirits of the Craters and the Eclipse
title.zh: 該亞與納拉：火山口之靈與日月蝕之禱

region.en: Mother and Daughters craters, Matupit, New Britain (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 新不列顛馬圖皮特對面的『母與女』火山口（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, 1910, ch. XIV

source.work: George Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians: Their Life-Histories Described and Compared (London: Macmillan, 1910), ch. XIV 'History, Mythology'

summary.en: The Kaia is the evil omnipresent spirit of New Britain: he afflicts people with deformity and disease, causes earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and calamity, and lives in craters and dark places; To Lagulagu is the particular Kaia of the craters called the Mother and Daughters opposite Matupit. Against him stands Nara — 'the certain one' — the good omnipresent spirit to whom the people pray in earthquake and eclipse: 'Nara i tara dat,' Nara, who made us; and of the mountains, 'Nara ku i pami,' Nara alone he made them.
summary.zh: 新不列顛人的『該亞』乃遍在之惡靈：致人殘疾疾病，興地震、火山與災禍，居於火山口與幽暗之地；馬圖皮特對面『母與女』火山口中的該亞名為托拉古拉古。與之相對是善靈『納拉』（意謂『那一位』）：地震與日月蝕之時，人們向納拉祈禱——『Nara i tara dat』（納拉造了我們）；論及群山則說『Nara ku i pami』（唯納拉造了它們）。

passages.text: The term Kaia (or Kaiya) was applied to an evil omnipresent and powerful spirit who afflicted people with deformity and diseases, was the cause of earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and other calamities, and lived in craters and dark places. The term was also applied to any evil spirit, a large snake or iguana that was much dreaded. To Lagulagu was the name of the particular Kaia who resided in the craters called the Mother and Daughters opposite the island of Matupit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was also a good omnipresent and powerful spirit called Nara. This word means a certain one, or it may have come from two words na (mother) and ra (one). They prayed to this Nara during an earthquake and also at an eclipse. When asked the reason for this they always replied, 'Nara i tara dat,' i.e. Nara, who made us, or it may have meant he who made us. Speaking of the mountains on New Britain they said, 'Nara ku i pami,' i.e. Nara alone he made them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brown, Melanesians and Polynesians, ch. XIV (1910); not verbatim.
